title: How the populist right profits from online misogyny
gist: Cynthia Miller-Idriss argues a global surge in misogyny among gen Z men is being engineered by an alignment of far-right politicians and monetised online influencers who game outrage-driven algorithms, and that misogyny is the strongest predictor of extremist beliefs and a throughline in mass violence. She contends social media bans barely work (Australia's under-16 ban cut use only 5 points) and calls for platform regulation, prebunking, peer interventions and cultural change, treating misogyny as a national-security issue.

insights.claim: Miller-Idriss argues gender has become one of the most powerful levers the illiberal and extreme right uses to mobilise voters and donors, from Hungary and Poland to Germany, France and the US.
insights.speaker: Cynthia Miller-Idriss
insights.so_what: Gender polarisation is a durable driver of far-right vote share; factor it into European and US political-risk models.

insights.claim: In the US 57% of men under 30 backed Trump in 2024, a significant jump from 2020, while most women under 30 voted for Kamala Harris; similar gaps fuel young men's support for the AfD in Germany.

insights.claim: Young white men swung to Democrats by a double-digit margin in the 2026 US midterms, but the author attributes this to economic dissatisfaction rather than rejection of Trump's strong-man stances.
insights.speaker: Cynthia Miller-Idriss
insights.so_what: Midterm swing among young men is economy-driven and reversible; don't read it as a values shift.

themes.theme: Monetised outrage: algorithms and the manosphere economy

insights.claim: Creators use gender outrage to game algorithms and monetise via ads, paid promotions and merchandise, cohering once-fringe grievances into organised narratives.
insights.speaker: Cynthia Miller-Idriss
insights.so_what: Engagement-driven ad models monetise misogynistic content, a regulatory and brand-safety liability for platforms.
insights.quote: creators use outrage over gender to game algorithms in ways that generate profit

insights.claim: Young men interviewed said manosphere content dominates their TikTok, Instagram and YouTube feeds even when they do not engage with or follow such influencers.
insights.speaker: Cynthia Miller-Idriss
insights.so_what: Recommendation systems push this content unsolicited, strengthening the case for algorithmic-design regulation.
insights.quote: the Andrew Tate manosphere was dominating my For You page
insights.locator: But this isn’t just a teenage algorithm problem.

insights.speaker: Cynthia Miller-Idriss
insights.so_what: Generative-AI image abuse is a live legal and regulatory risk for xAI and AI platforms generally.

insights.speaker: Cynthia Miller-Idriss
insights.so_what: New content restrictions raise compliance costs for adult-content platforms in the UK.

themes.theme: What works: bans vs prebunking and regulation

insights.claim: Australia's world-first under-16 social media ban, implemented late 2025, cut social media use among 10-15-year-olds by only 5 percentage points (86% to 81%) after three months.
insights.speaker: Cynthia Miller-Idriss
insights.so_what: Age bans have limited effect; expect policy to pivot toward platform-design and content regulation, a bigger compliance burden for platforms.
insights.quote: fell by only 5 percentage points, from 86 per cent before the ban to 81 per cent three months after
insights.locator: While less time online is good

insights.claim: The author calls for continued enforcement of the UK's 2023 Online Safety Act with heavy financial and criminal penalties, and for Ofcom's voluntary guidance on online harms to women to become binding regulation.
insights.speaker: Cynthia Miller-Idriss
insights.so_what: Watch for Ofcom converting voluntary guidance into rules — a compliance cost for social platforms operating in the UK.

insights.claim: A new Lancet report argues manosphere content causes health harms and should be treated with public-health interventions like tobacco and ultra-processed food.
insights.speaker: Cynthia Miller-Idriss
insights.so_what: A tobacco-style framing opens the door to restrictions on platforms like those placed on tobacco and junk-food advertising.
